title: Opinions and argument
objectives: I can give an opinion with 'Я ду́маю, що...', 'Я вважа́ю, що...', 'Мені́ здає́ться, що...' and 'на мою́ ду́мку', and ask for one with 'Як ти вважа́єш?' and 'Як ви вважа́єте?'.
I can agree and disagree politely with 'Я з тобо́ю пого́джуюся', 'Ти ма́єш ра́цію', 'Я так не вважа́ю', 'Я в цьо́му сумніва́юся' and 'Дозво́льте запере́чити'.
I can give a cause with 'бо', 'тому́ що' and 'оскі́льки', or with 'че́рез' and the accusative for a bad result and 'завдяки́' and the dative for a good one.
I can admit a point and set another against it with 'хоча́', 'незважа́ючи на', 'проте́' and 'одна́к', and draw a conclusion with 'тому́' and 'о́тже'.

I can build an argument with 'по-пе́рше', 'по-дру́ге', 'з одного́ бо́ку' and 'з і́ншого бо́ку', put commas around parenthetical words, and explain the hyphen in 'по-пе́рше', the soft 'ль' in 'суспі́льство' and the doubled 'л' in 'довкі́лля'.

vocabulary.note: It names both a thought that comes to you and an opinion you hold. Plural 'ду́мки'. Before the ending '-і' the 'к' becomes 'ц': 'у ду́мці', in one's thoughts.

example.target: Це ціка́ва ду́мка.
example.source: That's an interesting thought.

vocabulary.note: The preposition 'на' with the accusative 'мою́ ду́мку'. For another person change the possessive: 'на твою́ ду́мку', 'на ва́шу ду́мку', 'на його́ ду́мку'. It is a parenthetical phrase, so commas set it off.

example.target: На мою́ ду́мку, цей фільм ду́же до́вгий.
example.source: In my opinion, this film is very long.
example.source_literal: On my opinion, this film very long.

vocabulary.note: 'Вважа́ю', 'вважа́єш', like 'чита́ти'. With 'що' it gives a considered opinion, firmer than 'ду́мати'. With an accusative object and a description in the instrumental it means to consider someone or something to be: 'Я вважа́ю його́ до́брим дру́гом.' It has no perfective partner.

example.target: Я вважа́ю, що вам тре́ба відпочи́ти.
example.source: I believe you need to rest.
example.source_literal: I consider, that to-you necessary to-rest.

vocabulary.note: 'Пого́джуюся', 'пого́джуєшся', like 'працюва́ти': '-ува-' becomes '-у-'. Perfective partner 'погоди́тися'. The person or the idea agreed with follows 'з' with the instrumental. 'I agree' said now is always this imperfective: 'Я пого́джуюся.'

example.target: Оле́на ча́сто не пого́джується з бра́том.
example.source: Olena often disagrees with her brother.
example.source_literal: Olena often not agrees with brother.

vocabulary.note: 'Погоджу́ся', 'пого́дишся', 'пого́дяться': 'д' becomes 'дж' in the 'я' form. Imperfective partner 'пого́джуватися'. It names one act of agreeing, often after doubt or refusal. With an infinitive it means to agree to do something: 'Він погоди́вся допомогти́.'

example.target: Споча́тку ба́тько запере́чував, але́ наре́шті погоди́вся.
example.source: At first Dad objected, but in the end he agreed.

vocabulary.note: 'Запере́чую', 'запере́чуєш', like 'працюва́ти'. Perfective partner 'запере́чити' ('запере́чу', 'запере́чиш'). Without an object it means to object; with 'що' and a clause it means to deny. 'Не запере́чую.' is a polite 'I don't object'.

example.target: Він запере́чує, що взяв гро́ші.
example.source: He denies that he took the money.

vocabulary.note: 'Сумніва́юся', 'сумніва́єшся', like 'чита́ти'. It is built on the noun 'сумні́в', doubt. What you doubt follows 'у' or 'в' with the locative ('сумніва́тися в цьо́му') or 'що' with an ordinary verb. The perfective 'засумніва́тися' means to begin to doubt.

example.target: Я сумніва́юся, що за́втра бу́де те́пло.
example.source: I doubt it will be warm tomorrow.
example.source_literal: I doubt, that tomorrow will-be warm.

vocabulary.note: 'Ра́ція' is a feminine noun meaning reason, in the sense of being in the right, and in this sense it is met almost only in this phrase. 'Ма́ти' changes as usual: 'я ма́ю ра́цію', 'ви ма́єте ра́цію'. Ukrainian says that someone has reason, where English says that someone is right.

example.target: Ма́ма завжди́ ма́є ра́цію.
example.source: Mom is always right.

vocabulary.note: It numbers the first point of an argument; the next points are 'по-дру́ге' and 'по-тре́тє'. It is used as a parenthetical word, so a comma follows it. The note on spelling and sound explains the hyphen.

example.target: По-пе́рше, цей буди́нок ду́же стари́й.
example.source: Firstly, this building is very old.

vocabulary.note: 'Бік', side, has the genitive 'бо́ку', after 'з' meaning 'from'. The phrase opens the first side of a balanced argument, and 'з і́ншого бо́ку' opens the second. Commas set it off.

example.target: З одного́ бо́ку, мі́сто вели́ке й ціка́ве.
example.source: On the one hand, the city is big and interesting.
example.source_literal: From one side, city big and interesting.

vocabulary.note: It opens the second side of an argument, after 'з одного́ бо́ку' or on its own. 'З дру́гого бо́ку' is also used. Commas set it off.

example.target: З і́ншого бо́ку, жи́ти там ду́же до́рого.
example.source: On the other hand, living there is very expensive.
example.source_literal: From other side, to-live there very expensive.

vocabulary.note: It joins a statement that runs against the one before, like 'але́', but it is more formal. It stands after a comma between two clauses or at the head of a new sentence, and no comma follows it.

example.target: Кварти́ра мала́, проте́ зру́чна.
example.source: The apartment is small but comfortable.

vocabulary.note: It opens a clause that admits a fact; the other clause says what holds anyway. Either clause can come first, with a comma between them. The shorter form 'хоч' is also correct.

example.target: Хоча́ Сем із Кана́ди, він до́бре гово́рить украї́нською.
example.source: Although Sam is from Canada, he speaks Ukrainian well.
example.source_literal: Although Sam from Canada, he well speaks by-Ukrainian.

vocabulary.note: It introduces a cause, like 'тому́ що', but it is bookish: it belongs to writing and formal speech. Its clause often comes first, with a comma before the main clause. It is built from 'скі́льки', how much.

example.target: Оскі́льки музе́й зачи́нено, ми пі́демо в парк.
example.source: Since the museum is closed, we'll go to the park.
example.source_literal: Since museum closed, we will-go in park.

vocabulary.note: It draws a conclusion from what has been said. At the head of a closing sentence it is used as a parenthetical word and a comma follows it. It is more formal than 'тому́'.

example.target: О́тже, ми ї́демо в субо́ту.
example.source: So, we're leaving on Saturday.

vocabulary.note: It takes the accusative: 'незважа́ючи на дощ'. Before a whole clause it becomes 'незважа́ючи на те, що'. It is 'не' and 'зважа́ючи', the adverbial participle of 'зважа́ти на', to heed, so it literally means 'not heeding'. Commas set off the phrase it opens.

example.target: Незважа́ючи на сніг, ді́ти гуля́ли в па́рку.
example.source: Despite the snow, the children played in the park.
example.source_literal: Not-heeding on snow, children strolled in park.

vocabulary.note: It takes the dative and names a cause with a good result: 'завдяки́ дру́гові', 'завдяки́ вам'. It shares its root with 'дя́кую'. A cause with a bad result takes 'че́рез' instead.

example.target: Завдяки́ сестрі́ я знайшо́в цю робо́ту.
example.source: Thanks to my sister, I found this job.
example.source_literal: Thanks-to to-sister I found this job.

vocabulary.note: It sets what is really true against what seems true or what someone believes. It is written as one word. 'Спра́вді', really, is a different adverb, which confirms what was said. It is not a parenthetical word, so no comma follows it.

example.target: Наспра́вді він не лі́кар, а студе́нт.
example.source: In fact, he isn't a doctor but a student.
example.source_literal: In-fact he not doctor, but student.

vocabulary.note: The natural world around people: air, 'пові́тря', water, land, plants and animals. It is a neuter noun in '-я' after a doubled consonant, like 'життя́': genitive 'довкі́лля', dative 'довкі́ллю'. What harms it 'шко́дить' it, with the dative: 'шко́дити довкі́ллю', to harm the environment.

example.target: Ми пови́нні ду́мати про довкі́лля.
example.source: We must think about the environment.

vocabulary.note: The people of a country or a community taken together. Genitive 'суспі́льства'. Nouns with the suffix '-ство' name a group or a state, and they are neuter.

example.target: Це пита́ння важли́ве для всього́ суспі́льства.
example.source: This question is important for the whole of society.
example.source_literal: This question important for all of-society.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'села́', plural 'се́ла', with the stress moving to the stem. 'У селі́' means in a village or in the countryside, and 'у село́' to a village or to the countryside, as with 'у мі́сті' and 'у мі́сто'.

example.target: Моя́ бабу́ся живе́ в селі́.
example.source: My grandmother lives in a village.

vocabulary.note: It also means a machine. 'Ї́хати маши́ною' and 'ї́хати на маши́ні' both mean to go by car, as with 'авто́бусом' and 'на авто́бусі'. 'Автомобі́ль' is the more formal word.

example.target: У на́шій сім’ї́ нема́є маши́ни.
example.source: Our family doesn't have a car.

dialogues.title: City or country?
dialogues.context: Over coffee at Andrii's café, Taras tells Oksana and Sam that he wants to leave Kyiv for a village. The three are friends and say 'ти' to each other, and 'ви' when Taras speaks to both at once. 'Ти́хо', 'галасли́во' and 'ва́жко' are predicative words made from 'ти́хий', 'галасли́вий' and 'важки́й', as 'хо́лодно' is made from 'холо́дний'. 'Дої́хати' is to reach a place by vehicle, with the prefix 'до-' of 'дійти́'.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Зна́єте, я хо́чу переї́хати з Ки́єва в село́.
lines.source: You know, I want to move from Kyiv to a village.
lines.source_literal: You-know, I want to-move from Kyiv into village.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У село́? Чому́?
lines.source: To a village? Why?
lines.source_literal: Into village? Why?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: По-пе́рше, я працю́ю вдо́ма, тому́ мені́ не тре́ба жи́ти в мі́сті. По-дру́ге, у селі́ ти́хо, а в мі́сті ду́же галасли́во.
lines.source: Firstly, I work from home, so I don't need to live in the city. Secondly, it's quiet in a village, and the city is very noisy.
lines.source_literal: Firstly, I work at-home, so to-me not necessary to-live in city. Secondly, in village quiet, and in city very noisy.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я з тобо́ю пого́джуюся. Мені́ здає́ться, що в селі́ лю́ди ма́ють бі́льше ча́су.
lines.source: I agree with you. It seems to me that people in a village have more time.
lines.source_literal: I with you agree. To-me seems, that in village people have more of-time.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я так не вважа́ю. Хоча́ в селі́ ти́хо, там нема́є до́брої лі́карні.
lines.source: Well, I don't think so. Although it's quiet in a village, there's no good hospital there.
lines.source_literal: And I so not consider. Although in village quiet, there there-is-not of-good of-hospital.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Наспра́вді в мало́му мі́сті по́руч є лі́карня.
lines.source: Actually, there's a hospital in a small town nearby.
lines.source_literal: In-fact in small town nearby is hospital.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Мо́жливо. Але́ взи́мку че́рез сніг туди́ ва́жко дої́хати.
lines.source: Maybe. But in winter it's hard to get there because of the snow.
lines.source_literal: Possibly. But in-winter because-of snow there hard to-reach.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: З одного́ бо́ку, ти ма́єш ра́цію, Окса́но. З і́ншого бо́ку, Тара́сові не тре́ба щодня́ ї́здити на робо́ту.
lines.source: On the one hand, you're right, Oksana. On the other hand, Taras doesn't need to travel to work every day.
lines.source_literal: From one side, you have reason, Oksana. From other side, to-Taras not necessary every-day to-travel to work.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Дя́кую, Се́ме! О́тже, я ма́ю ра́цію.
lines.source: Thanks, Sam! So I'm right.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, Sam! So, I have reason.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я сумніва́юся, що тобі́ там сподо́бається. Ти так лю́биш мі́сто!
lines.source: Well, I doubt you'll like it there. You love the city so much!
lines.source_literal: And I doubt, that to-you there will-please. You so love city!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Незважа́ючи на все, я хо́чу жи́ти в селі́.
lines.source: Despite everything, I want to live in a village.
lines.source_literal: Not-heeding on everything, I want to-live in village.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тоді́ ми бу́демо приїжджа́ти до те́бе на вихідні́.
lines.source: Then we'll come and visit you on weekends.
lines.source_literal: Then we will-be to-come to you on weekend.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А ти бу́деш приїжджа́ти до нас, бо в селі́ нема́є кафе́ Андрі́я!
lines.source: And you'll come to see us, because there's no Andrii's café in a village!
lines.source_literal: And you will-be to-come to us, because in village there-is-not café of-Andrii!

dialogues.title: Can you learn a language online?
dialogues.context: In Iryna Petrivna's Ukrainian class, Oksana is again a guest who helps the foreign students practice conversation. Today the class discusses learning languages online: 'онла́йн' is a word taken from English that never changes its form, and 'уро́к' means a lesson. Iryna Petrivna and her adult students say 'ви' to each other; Sam and Oksana are friends and say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Сього́дні на́ше пита́ння таке́: чи мо́жна до́бре вивча́ти мо́ву онла́йн? Се́ме, як ви вважа́єте?
lines.source: Today our question is this: can you learn a language well online? Sam, what do you think?
lines.source_literal: Today our question such: whether possible well to-study language online? Sam, how you consider?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: На мою́ ду́мку, мо́жна. Я ча́сто вивча́ю нові́ слова́ на телефо́ні, бо це зру́чно.
lines.source: In my opinion, you can. I often learn new words on my phone, because it's convenient.
lines.source_literal: On my opinion, possible. I often study new words on phone, because this convenient.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А розмо́ва? Мені́ здає́ться, що говори́ти ле́гше з люди́ною, ніж із телефо́ном.
lines.source: And conversation? It seems to me that it's easier to talk with a person than with a phone.
lines.source_literal: And conversation? To-me seems, that to-speak easier with person, than with phone.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я з ва́ми пого́джуюся, Іри́но Петрі́вно. Хоча́ я вивча́ю англі́йську онла́йн, говори́ти англі́йською мені́ допомага́є Сем.
lines.source: I agree with you, Iryna Petrivna. Although I study English online, it's Sam who helps me speak English.
lines.source_literal: I with you agree, Iryna Petrivna. Although I study English online, to-speak by-English to-me helps Sam.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, але́ завдяки́ уро́кам онла́йн ти зна́єш бага́то слів.
lines.source: Yes, but thanks to your online lessons you know a lot of words.
lines.source_literal: Yes, but thanks-to to-lessons online you know many of-words.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ти ма́єш ра́цію. О́тже, онла́йн кра́ще вивча́ти слова́ й грама́тику, а говори́ти кра́ще з люди́ною.
lines.source: You're right. So online is better for learning words and grammar, and talking is better with a person.
lines.source_literal: You have reason. So, online better to-study words and grammar, and to-speak better with person.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. А хто ду́має іна́кше?
lines.source: Very good. And who thinks differently?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дозво́льте запере́чити, Іри́но Петрі́вно. Наспра́вді онла́йн я теж говорю́ з людьми́. У ме́не є по́друга з Ха́ркова, і ми гово́римо ко́жен ти́ждень.
lines.source: Allow me to object, Iryna Petrivna. In fact, I also talk with people online. I have a friend from Kharkiv, and we talk every week.
lines.source_literal: Allow to-object, Iryna Petrivna. In-fact online I also speak with people. At me is friend from Kharkiv, and we speak every week.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ціка́во! Тоді́ я з ва́ми погоджу́ся. Важли́во не те, де ми гово́римо, а те, що ми гово́римо ча́сто.
lines.source: Interesting! Then I'll agree with you. What matters is not where we talk, but that we talk often.
lines.source_literal: Interesting! Then I with you will-agree. Important not that, where we speak, but that, that we speak often.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: О́тже, сього́дні ми всі ма́ємо ра́цію!
lines.source: So today we're all right!
lines.source_literal: So, today we all have reason!

grammar.title: Giving and asking for an opinion: що and the indicative
grammar.explanation:
An opinion is a statement that the speaker presents as their own view rather than as a plain fact. Ukrainian gives an opinion the way English does: a verb of thinking, then a clause that says what is thought. The clause opens with 'що', that, and a comma always stands before 'що'. English often drops 'that' ('I think it will rain'); a full Ukrainian sentence keeps 'що': 'Я ду́маю, що бу́де дощ.' Without 'що', 'ду́маю' becomes a parenthetical comment set off by a comma, like 'здає́ться': 'Ду́маю, у це́нтрі.' (In the center, I think.)

The verb in the clause with 'що' is the ordinary indicative, in the tense it would have if the clause stood alone as a statement. This is where it differs from a clause with 'щоб'. After a wish or a request for another person, the clause takes 'щоб' and the past form, because it describes something not yet real. An opinion describes the world as the speaker believes it is, so it keeps the ordinary verb:

- 'Я ду́маю, що Сем при́йде.' (I think Sam will come.) states a belief, with the future 'при́йде'.
- 'Я хо́чу, щоб Сем прийшо́в.' (I want Sam to come.) states a wish, with 'щоб' and the past form 'прийшо́в'.

Hope, fear and doubt also take 'що' and the indicative: 'Я сумніва́юся, що він при́йде.' (I doubt he will come.)

Four openers give an opinion:

- 'Я ду́маю, що...' is the everyday choice.
- 'Я вважа́ю, що...' gives a considered view; it is common in discussions and in writing.
- 'На мою́ ду́мку,...' (in my opinion) is the preposition 'на' with the accusative of 'моя́ ду́мка'. It is a parenthetical phrase: it stands outside the grammar of the sentence, so commas set it off. For another person, change the possessive: 'на твою́ ду́мку', 'на ва́шу ду́мку'.
- 'Мені́ здає́ться, що...' (it seems to me that) is the softest. The person is in the dative, and the verb 'здава́тися', to seem, is in the 'він' form, because what seems is the whole clause with 'що', not the person. It works like 'Мені́ подо́бається': the person is not the subject. Without 'мені́', 'Здає́ться, що...' means 'It seems that...'. Set off by commas inside a sentence, 'здає́ться' is the parenthetical word of the A2 consolidation unit ('Він, здає́ться, удо́ма.').

'Вважа́ти' has a second pattern without 'що': an accusative object and a description in the instrumental, the case of a role ('Він працю́є лі́карем'). 'Я вважа́ю цей фільм ціка́вим.' means 'I consider this film interesting'.

To ask for an opinion, Ukrainian says 'how', where English says 'what': 'Як ти вважа́єш?' or 'Як ви вважа́єте?' (What do you think?). 'Що ти ду́маєш про...?' takes 'про' with the accusative: 'Що ти ду́маєш про цей фільм?' The most direct question is 'Яка́ твоя́ ду́мка?' (What is your opinion?).

examples.target: Я ду́маю, що за́втра бу́де дощ.
examples.source: I think it will rain tomorrow.
examples.source_literal: I think, that tomorrow will-be rain.

examples.target: Я вважа́ю, що ді́тям тре́ба бага́то спа́ти.
examples.source: I believe children need a lot of sleep.
examples.source_literal: I consider, that to-children necessary much to-sleep.

examples.target: Мені́ здає́ться, що Окса́на вже вдо́ма.

grammar.title: Agreeing and disagreeing
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian expresses agreement with a verb, 'пого́джуватися', with the person or the idea you agree with after 'з' in the instrumental: 'Я з тобо́ю пого́джуюся.' (I agree with you.) 'З тобо́ю' may also follow the verb: 'Я пого́джуюся з тобо́ю.' 'I agree' said now is always the imperfective 'пого́джуюся', because it describes a present state. The perfective 'погоди́тися' names one act of agreeing, usually after doubt or refusal: 'Ба́тько погоди́вся.' (Dad agreed.) With an infinitive it means to agree to do something: 'Він погоди́вся допомогти́.' (He agreed to help.)

Two other ways to agree are just as common:

- 'Ти ма́єш ра́цію.' (You're right.) is literally 'you have reason': Ukrainian says that a person has 'ра́ція', where English says that a person is right. 'Ма́ти' changes as usual: 'Ви ма́єте ра́цію.', 'Вона́ ма́є ра́цію.'
- 'Я зго́ден.' (said by a man) and 'Я зго́дна.' (said by a woman) mean 'I agree'. 'Зго́ден' is a short adjective used as a predicate, like 'пови́нен', and it agrees with the subject: 'зго́ден', 'зго́дна', 'зго́дні'. It comes from 'зго́да', agreement, which shares its root with 'погоди́тися'.

Disagreement is usually softened. These are the common ways to disagree, from the gentlest to the bluntest:

- 'Я так не вважа́ю.' (I don't think so.)
- 'Я в цьо́му сумніва́юся.' (I doubt it.) 'Сумніва́тися' takes 'у' or 'в' with the locative.
- 'Я з тобо́ю не пого́джуюся.' (I don't agree with you.)
- 'Дозво́льте запере́чити.' (Allow me to object.) is formal, for a teacher, a meeting or someone you call 'ви'. 'Дозво́льте' is the imperative of 'дозво́лити', the perfective of 'дозволя́ти', and 'запере́чити' is the perfective of 'запере́чувати'.
- 'Ти не ма́єш ра́ції.' (You're wrong.) is direct and is said mostly among friends.

In the last sentence 'ра́ція' is in the genitive, 'ра́ції'. When 'ма́ти' is negated, its object usually goes into the genitive, as after 'нема́є': 'Я не ма́ю ча́су.' (I have no time.), 'Він не ма́є до́свіду.' (He has no experience.)

A good way to disagree politely is to grant part of the other person's point first: 'Ти ма́єш ра́цію, але́...' (You're right, but...). The notes below give the words that do this inside one sentence.

grammar.title: Giving a cause: бо, тому́ що, оскі́льки, че́рез and завдяки́
grammar.explanation:
A cause answers the question 'чому́?', why. Ukrainian gives it in one of two ways: as a whole clause with its own verb, opened by a conjunction, or as a single noun, after a preposition.

Three conjunctions open a clause of cause. A comma always separates it from the main clause.

- 'бо' is the conversational word. Its clause comes after the main statement, and in writing it never opens a sentence: 'Я не прийшо́в, бо хворі́в.'
- 'тому́ що' is neutral, for speech and writing. Its clause usually follows the main statement, and on its own it answers 'Чому́?': 'Тому́ що йшов дощ.'
- 'оскі́льки' is bookish, used in writing and formal speech. Its clause often comes first, so that the reason is given before the result: 'Оскі́льки в ме́не нема́є ча́су, я не мо́жу допомогти́.'

Two prepositions give a cause as a noun, and they divide causes by their result:

- 'че́рез' with the accusative names a cause that led to something unwelcome: 'че́рез дощ' (because of the rain), 'че́рез ме́не' (because of me). It is the same preposition as in 'перейти́ че́рез ву́лицю' (across the street) and 'че́рез ти́ждень' (in a week), and in every meaning it takes the accusative.
- 'завдяки́' with the dative names a cause that led to something good, one the speaker is grateful for: 'завдяки́ дру́зям' (thanks to friends), 'завдяки́ вам' (thanks to you). It shares its root with 'дя́кую', so it is not used for a bad result.

A preposition cannot be followed by a clause directly. When the cause is a whole clause, the pronoun 'те' stands in for it, in the case the preposition requires, and the clause follows after a comma and 'що'. You met the same device in 'те, що' and in 'для того́, щоб':

- 'че́рез те, що' (because of the fact that), with 'те' in the accusative
- 'завдяки́ тому́, що' (thanks to the fact that), with 'тому́' in the dative

In 'тому́ що' the first word is in fact this same pronoun in the dative, followed by 'що'. It has fused with 'що' into a single conjunction meaning 'because'.

grammar.title: Concession and contrast: хоча́, незважа́ючи на, проте́ and одна́к
grammar.explanation:
A concession admits a fact that seems to stand against the main statement and then says that the main statement holds anyway. English uses 'although' and 'despite'. Ukrainian has the same two tools, a conjunction for a clause and a preposition for a noun.

- 'хоча́' (or the shorter 'хоч') opens a clause with its own verb: 'Хоча́ було́ хо́лодно, ми гуля́ли.' (Although it was cold, we went for a walk.) Either clause can come first, with a comma between them: 'Ми гуля́ли, хоча́ було́ хо́лодно.'
- 'незважа́ючи на' is followed by a noun or pronoun in the accusative: 'Незважа́ючи на сніг, ми гуля́ли.' (Despite the snow, we went for a walk.) It is built from 'не' and 'зважа́ючи', the adverbial participle of 'зважа́ти на', to heed, so it says 'not heeding the snow'. That is why it takes 'на' and the accusative, as 'зважа́ти' does. Commas set off the phrase it opens.
- Before a whole clause it becomes 'незважа́ючи на те, що', with 'те' standing in for the clause, as in the note on cause: 'Незважа́ючи на те, що йшов сніг, ми гуля́ли.' (Even though it was snowing, we went for a walk.)

A contrast does the same job from the other side. Instead of marking the admitted fact, it marks the statement that goes against it. 'Але́', but, is the everyday word. 'Проте́' and 'одна́к', both meaning 'however', are more formal and are common in writing, where they also avoid repeating 'але́':

- Between two clauses, after a comma: 'Було́ хо́лодно, проте́ ми гуля́ли.'
- At the head of a new sentence, with no comma after them: 'Було́ хо́лодно. Одна́к ми гуля́ли.'

So the same two facts can be joined in three ways, and the meaning stays the same: 'Хоча́ було́ хо́лодно, ми гуля́ли.', 'Незважа́ючи на хо́лод, ми гуля́ли.' and 'Було́ хо́лодно, проте́ ми гуля́ли.' The difference is which fact carries the marker. 'Хоча́' and 'незважа́ючи на' go with the fact that is admitted, while 'проте́', 'одна́к' and 'але́' go with the fact that wins. In the second of these sentences 'хо́лод' is the noun for cold, stressed on its first syllable.

grammar.title: Consequence and the structure of an argument; commas around parenthetical words
grammar.explanation:
Cause and consequence point in opposite directions. A word of cause introduces the reason, while a word of consequence introduces the result, and the result comes second:

- 'тому́' (so, that's why) introduces a result after the cause has been given: 'Ішо́в дощ, тому́ ми сиді́ли вдо́ма.' (It was raining, so we stayed at home.) Compare 'тому́ що', which introduces the cause: 'Ми сиді́ли вдо́ма, тому́ що йшов дощ.'
- 'о́тже' (so, therefore) draws a conclusion from everything said before it, and so it often opens the last sentence of an argument: 'О́тже, кра́ще жи́ти бли́зько до робо́ти.' It is more formal than 'тому́'.

An argument is easier to follow when its points are numbered and its sides are balanced. Ukrainian uses these words:

- 'по-пе́рше', 'по-дру́ге', 'по-тре́тє' (firstly, secondly, thirdly) number the points
- 'з одного́ бо́ку' (on the one hand, literally 'from one side') opens the first side
- 'з і́ншого бо́ку' (on the other hand, literally 'from other side') opens the second side

These words, like 'на мою́ ду́мку', are parenthetical. A parenthetical word or phrase is not part of the grammar of the sentence: it comments on the sentence from outside, saying what the speaker thinks of it, where it stands in the argument or how sure the speaker is. A test shows it: remove the word, and the sentence is still complete and correct. Ukrainian always sets a parenthetical word off with commas. At the start of a sentence one comma follows it, and in the middle one comma stands on each side: 'Ця кни́га, на мою́ ду́мку, ду́же ціка́ва.' These are the parenthetical words met so far:

- 'по-пе́рше', 'по-дру́ге', 'по-тре́тє'
- 'з одного́ бо́ку', 'з і́ншого бо́ку'
- 'на мою́ ду́мку', 'здає́ться', 'мо́же', 'мо́жливо'
- 'звича́йно', 'на жаль', 'до ре́чі', 'напри́клад'
- 'о́тже', when it opens a conclusion

Not every linking word is parenthetical. 'Тому́', 'проте́' and 'наспра́вді' belong to the grammar of their clause, so no comma follows them. 'Наспра́вді' (in fact) sets the truth against an appearance: 'Здає́ться, що це ле́гко, але́ наспра́вді це ва́жко.' (It seems easy, but in fact it is hard.) 'Спра́вді' (really, indeed) does the opposite and confirms what was said: 'Це спра́вді ва́жко.' (It really is hard.)

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: по-пе́рше, суспі́льство, довкі́лля and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit is read with the procedure of the alphabet units: find the vowels, find the stress mark, then decide for each consonant whether it is hard or soft. Three spellings deserve a closer look, and the other words apply rules you already know.

'По-пе́рше' is written with a hyphen. Ukrainian writes adverbs made of 'по' and a form of an adjective or an ordinal numeral with a hyphen, as in 'по-украї́нськи' from the unit on the instrumental. The ordinals give 'по-пе́рше', 'по-дру́ге' and 'по-тре́тє'. The two parts are said as one word with one stress, [pɔ ˈpɛrʃɛ]. 'По' has one syllable, so only the second part carries a mark. In 'по-тре́тє' the letter 'є' after 'т' shows that the 'т' is soft, as in the ordinal 'тре́тій', which has soft endings.

'Суспі́льство' is said [susˈpʲilʲstʋɔ]. The 'п' is soft before 'і'. The soft sign shows that the 'л' is soft before the consonant 'с', as in 'Львів'. Then comes the cluster 'ств', and every letter in it is sounded. The same soft sign before a consonant appears in 'оскі́льки' [ɔsˈkʲilʲkɪ].

'Довкі́лля' is said [dɔwˈkʲilʲːɑ]. The 'в' ends the syllable 'дов-' before a consonant, so it is [w], as in 'Петрі́вна'. The doubled 'лл' before 'я' is one long soft sound. It is the pattern of the neuter nouns in '-я' after a doubled consonant: 'життя́', 'столі́ття', 'насе́лення', 'пита́ння'.

The other new words apply known rules:

- In 'о́тже' [ˈɔdʒɛ] the voiceless 'т' becomes voiced [d] before the voiced 'ж', as 'к' becomes [ɡ] before 'з' in 'вокза́л'. The spelling keeps 'т'.
- In 'наспра́вді' [nɑˈsprɑwdʲi] and 'завдяки́' [zɑwdʲɑˈkɪ] the 'в' before a consonant is [w], and the 'д' is soft before 'і' and 'я'.
- 'Бік' becomes 'бо́ку' in 'з одного́ бо́ку': 'і' in a closed syllable, 'о' when an ending opens it, as in 'кіт', 'кота́'.
- 'Погоди́тися' has 'дж' in the 'я' form, 'погоджу́ся', as 'ходи́ти' has 'ходжу́'. The imperfective 'пого́джуватися' is built on that form and keeps 'дж' everywhere.
- 'Незважа́ючи' is one word because it is a preposition. The adverbial participle with 'не' is written as two words: 'Він ішо́в, не зважа́ючи на дощ.' (He walked on, paying no heed to the rain.)
- In 'ра́цію' [ˈrɑt͡sʲiju] the 'ц' is soft before 'і', and 'ю' after a vowel is [ju].
- 'Село́' moves its stress in the plural: 'се́ла'.
- In 'пого́джується', 'сумніва́ється' and 'здає́ться' the ending '-ться' is said [t͡sʲːɑ], one long soft 'ц'; in 'сумніва́єшся' the ending '-шся' is said [sʲːɑ], one long soft 'с', as in the reflexive verbs of the daily-routine unit.
- 'Онла́йн' [ɔnˈlɑjn] is taken from English and never changes its form.

culture.title: Arguing well: the school essay, polite disagreement and 'толо́ка'
culture.text:
Ukrainian schools teach students to write a short argument. For many years the external school-leaving exam in Ukrainian language and literature, which students took to enter university, ended with exactly such a text: the student stated a thesis, supported it with arguments and with examples from literature, history or life, and finished with a conclusion. Students learned linking words as a fixed frame for that task:

- 'На мою́ ду́мку,...' or 'Я вважа́ю, що...' to state the thesis
- 'По-пе́рше,...' and 'По-дру́ге,...' to introduce the arguments
- 'Напри́клад,...' to give an example
- 'О́тже,...' to draw the conclusion

In conversation, Ukrainians usually soften disagreement, especially with someone they call 'ви'. A speaker often grants part of the other person's point before opposing it ('Ви ма́єте ра́цію, але́...'), or presents a different view as a personal one with the conditional of the A2 unit: 'Я б сказа́в іна́кше.' (I would put it differently.) In a meeting or a class, 'Дозво́льте запере́чити.' or 'Дозво́льте не погоди́тися.' (Allow me to disagree.) sound respectful. Among friends, a direct 'Ти не ма́єш ра́ції!' is normal and is not taken as rude.

Many public debates in Ukraine today concern 'суспі́льство' and 'довкі́лля': cars and public transport in city centers, clean rivers, and life in villages against life in cities. An old word has found a new use here. 'Толо́ка' was the village custom of neighbors working together, without pay, on a job too big for one family, such as building a house or bringing in the harvest. Today the same word names a community clean-up day, when neighbors clean a park, a courtyard or a riverbank together.

paragraphs.source: Of course, a car is convenient. However, Kyiv has buses and the metro, and in the center everything is close.

paragraphs.target: В і́нших міста́х Євро́пи маши́нам уже́ заборо́нено в’їжджа́ти в центр. Незважа́ючи на те, що споча́тку бага́то люде́й запере́чували, за́раз їм таке́ мі́сто подо́бається.
paragraphs.source: In other European cities, cars are already forbidden to enter the center. Even though many people objected at first, they now like such a city.
paragraphs.source_literal: In other cities of-Europe to-cars already forbidden to-drive-in into center. Not-heeding on that, that at-first many of-people objected, now to-them such city pleases.

paragraphs.target: О́тже, я вважа́ю, що маши́нам тре́ба заборони́ти в’їжджа́ти в центр Ки́єва. Завдяки́ цьому́ центр ста́не ти́хим і зру́чним, а це до́бре для всього́ суспі́льства.
paragraphs.source: So I believe that cars should be banned from entering the center of Kyiv. Thanks to this, the center will become quiet and comfortable, and that is good for the whole of society.
paragraphs.source_literal: So, I consider, that to-cars necessary to-forbid to-drive-in into center of-Kyiv. Thanks-to to-this center will-become quiet and comfortable, and this good for all of-society.

questions.prompt: What is the author's main opinion?
choices: Kyiv needs more cars in its center.
Cars should not be allowed to enter the center of Kyiv.
Buses should be banned from the center of Kyiv.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the conclusion: 'маши́нам тре́ба заборони́ти в’їжджа́ти в центр Ки́єва'.

questions.prompt: What is the author's second argument, introduced by 'по-дру́ге'?
choices: Cars leave little room for people on the streets.
Cars are expensive.
The metro is noisy.
questions.explanation: 'По-дру́ге, че́рез маши́ни на ву́лицях ма́ло мі́сця для люде́й.' The first argument, after 'по-пе́рше', is the harm to the environment.

questions.prompt: What happened in other European cities, according to the fourth paragraph?
choices: People never objected to the ban.
People objected and the ban was lifted.
Many people objected at first, but now they like the car-free center.
questions.explanation: 'Незважа́ючи на те, що споча́тку бага́то люде́й запере́чували, за́раз їм таке́ мі́сто подо́бається.' The clause with 'незважа́ючи на те, що' admits the objection, and the main clause says what holds anyway.

questions.prompt: Which word in the third paragraph introduces the author's answer to the point that a car is convenient?
choices: Звича́йно
Проте́
Бли́зько
questions.explanation: 'Звича́йно' grants the point, and 'проте́' introduces the statement that goes against it.

paragraphs.target: Мене́ зва́ти Со́фія, і я програмі́стка. Уже́ два ро́ки я працю́ю вдо́ма, і, на мою́ ду́мку, це ду́же зру́чно.
paragraphs.source: My name is Sofiia, and I am a programmer. I have been working from home for two years now, and in my opinion it is very convenient.
paragraphs.source_literal: Me to-call Sofiia, and I programmer. Already two years I work at-home, and, on my opinion, this very convenient.

paragraphs.target: По-пе́рше, мені́ не тре́ба щодня́ ї́здити на робо́ту, тому́ в ме́не бі́льше ча́су для сім’ї́. По-дру́ге, завдяки́ робо́ті вдо́ма я ме́нше ї́жджу маши́ною, а це до́бре для довкі́лля.
paragraphs.source: Firstly, I don't have to travel to work every day, so I have more time for my family. Secondly, thanks to working from home I drive less, and that is good for the environment.
paragraphs.source_literal: Firstly, to-me not necessary every-day to-travel to work, so at me more of-time for family. Secondly, thanks-to to-work at-home I less travel by-car, and this good for environment.

paragraphs.target: Хоча́ я не ба́чу коле́г щодня́, ми до́бре працю́ємо ра́зом. О́тже, робо́та вдо́ма ма́є майбу́тнє.
paragraphs.source: Although I don't see my colleagues every day, we work well together. So working from home has a future.
paragraphs.source_literal: Although I not see of-colleagues every-day, we well work together. So, work at-home has future.

paragraphs.target: Я інжене́р. Я прочита́в лист па́ні Со́фії й хо́чу запере́чити. Звича́йно, працюва́ти вдо́ма зру́чно. Проте́ я вважа́ю, що лю́дям тре́ба працюва́ти ра́зом, в одному́ мі́сці.
paragraphs.source: I am an engineer. I read Ms. Sofiia's letter, and I want to object. Of course, working from home is convenient. However, I believe that people need to work together, in one place.
paragraphs.source_literal: I engineer. I read letter Ms. of-Sofiia and want to-object. Of-course, to-work at-home convenient. However I consider, that to-people necessary to-work together, in one place.

paragraphs.target: По-пе́рше, молоді́ співробі́тники ще не ма́ють до́свіду, а вдо́ма їм ніхто́ не допомага́є. По-дру́ге, я сумніва́юся, що коле́ги, які́ ніко́ли не зустріча́ються, мо́жуть ста́ти дру́зями.
paragraphs.source: Firstly, young employees do not yet have experience, and at home nobody helps them. Secondly, I doubt that colleagues who never meet can become friends.
paragraphs.source_literal: Firstly, young employees yet not have of-experience, and at-home to-them nobody not helps. Secondly, I doubt, that colleagues, who never not meet, can to-become by-friends.

questions.prompt: Why does Sofiia have more time for her family?
choices: She works fewer hours.
She does not have to travel to work every day.
Her colleagues help her at home.
questions.explanation: 'Мені́ не тре́ба щодня́ ї́здити на робо́ту, тому́ в ме́не бі́льше ча́су для сім’ї́.' 'Тому́' introduces the result.

questions.prompt: Which of Sofiia's arguments concerns the environment?
choices: She drives less.
She sees her colleagues every day.
She lives in a village.
questions.explanation: 'Завдяки́ робо́ті вдо́ма я ме́нше ї́жджу маши́ною, а це до́бре для довкі́лля.'

questions.prompt: According to the second letter, why is working from home hard for young employees?
choices: They have no computer at home.
They earn too little.
They have no experience yet, and nobody helps them at home.
questions.explanation: 'Молоді́ співробі́тники ще не ма́ють до́свіду, а вдо́ма їм ніхто́ не допомага́є.' After the negated 'ма́ють', 'до́свід' is in the genitive.

questions.prompt: How can you tell that the second letter was written by a man?
choices: He uses the past form 'прочита́в', which ends in '-в'.
He signs his name.
He writes 'па́ні Со́фії'.
questions.explanation: The past form agrees with its subject in gender: 'я прочита́в' is said by a man, and a woman would write 'я прочита́ла'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings

choices: I'm waiting for you.
I agree with you.
I don't agree with you.

exercises.prompt: How do you tell a friend 'You're right'?
choices: Ти ма́єш час.
Ти сумніва́єшся.
Ти ма́єш ра́цію.
exercises.explanation: 'Ма́ти ра́цію' is literally 'to have reason'. 'Ти ма́єш час.' means 'You have time', and 'Ти сумніва́єшся.' means 'You doubt'.

exercises.prompt: Match the linking words with their meanings

exercises.audio_target: На мою́ ду́мку, це ду́же до́рого.
choices: In my opinion, it's very expensive.
In my opinion, it's very far.
In my opinion, it's very cheap.

exercises.explanation: An opinion is a verb of thinking followed by 'що' and a clause. 'Вважа́ю' gives a considered view; 'ду́маю' is the everyday word.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Я ду́маю, ___ він при́йде.' (I think he will come.)?
choices: щоб
що
якби́
exercises.explanation: An opinion takes 'що' and the ordinary indicative, here the future 'при́йде'. 'Щоб' with the past form follows a wish or a request: 'Я хо́чу, щоб він прийшо́в.'

exercises.hint_source: I consider this book very interesting.
exercises.explanation: Without 'що', 'вважа́ти' takes an accusative object, 'цю кни́гу', and a description in the instrumental, the feminine 'ціка́вою'.
'Пого́джуватися' changes like 'працюва́ти', so the 'вона́' form is 'пого́джується'. The people agreed with follow 'з' in the instrumental, 'з на́ми'.

exercises.prompt_target: Ми до́вго проси́ли, і ма́ма наре́шті ___.
exercises.hint_source: We asked for a long time, and Mom finally agreed.
exercises.explanation: One act of agreeing with a result is the perfective 'погоди́тися', here in the feminine past. After the vowel '-а' the suffix can be '-ся' or '-сь'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence disagrees politely with someone you call 'ви'?
choices: Дозво́льте запере́чити.
Ти не ма́єш ра́ції.
Ви ма́єте ра́цію.
exercises.explanation: 'Дозво́льте запере́чити.' (Allow me to object.) is the formal way to disagree. 'Ти не ма́єш ра́ції.' is blunt and uses 'ти', and 'Ви ма́єте ра́цію.' agrees.

exercises.hint_source: We didn't go for a walk because of the rain.
exercises.explanation: A cause with an unwelcome result is 'че́рез' with the accusative, here 'дощ'.
A cause with a good result is 'завдяки́' with the dative, here 'тобі́'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'че́рез дощ' but 'завдяки́ дру́зям'?
choices: 'Че́рез' is used only with things and 'завдяки́' only with people.
'Че́рез' names a cause with a bad result and takes the accusative; 'завдяки́' names a cause with a good result and takes the dative.
'Че́рез' is formal and 'завдяки́' is conversational.
exercises.explanation: The choice depends on the result. 'Завдяки́' shares its root with 'дя́кую', so it is used only for something the speaker is glad of.

exercises.audio_target: Незважа́ючи на сніг, Тара́с пої́хав у село́.
choices: Despite the rain, Taras went to the village.
Despite the snow, Taras went to the city.
Despite the snow, Taras went to the village.
The genitive
The dative
The accusative
exercises.explanation: 'Незважа́ючи' is the adverbial participle of 'зважа́ти на', to heed, which takes 'на' with the accusative: 'незважа́ючи на дощ', 'незважа́ючи на те, що...'.

exercises.prompt_target: ___ в ме́не ма́ло гро́шей, я куплю́ тобі́ пода́рунок.
exercises.hint_source: Although I have little money, I'll buy you a present.
exercises.explanation: 'Хоча́' opens the clause that admits a fact; the main clause says what happens anyway.

exercises.hint_source: The apartment is old, but very bright.
exercises.explanation: A statement that runs against the one before follows 'але́', or the more formal 'проте́' or 'одна́к', after a comma.

exercises.prompt_target: Незважа́ючи на ___, що Тара́с хворі́в, він прийшо́в на вечі́рку.
exercises.hint_source: Even though Taras was ill, he came to the party.
exercises.explanation: A preposition cannot take a clause directly, so 'те' in the accusative stands in for it: 'незважа́ючи на те, що'.

exercises.prompt: In which sentence does 'тому́' introduce a result?
choices: Ішо́в дощ, тому́ ми сиді́ли вдо́ма.
Ми сиді́ли вдо́ма, тому́ що йшов дощ.
Ми були́ там рік тому́.
exercises.explanation: 'Тому́' alone introduces the result, after the cause. 'Тому́ що' introduces the cause, and 'рік тому́' means 'a year ago'.

exercises.prompt: Why is there a comma after 'по-пе́рше' in 'По-пе́рше, це до́рого.'?
choices: It is a parenthetical word, which is always set off by commas.
It is a conjunction, and a comma follows every conjunction.
A comma follows the first word of every sentence that has a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: A parenthetical word comments on the sentence from outside and can be removed without breaking it, so commas set it off. A conjunction such as 'проте́' at the head of a sentence takes no comma.

exercises.prompt_target: З одного́ ___, жи́ти в мі́сті ціка́во.
exercises.hint_source: On the one hand, living in the city is interesting.
exercises.explanation: 'З одного́ бо́ку' is literally 'from one side'. 'Бік' has the genitive 'бо́ку': 'і' in the closed syllable becomes 'о' when the ending opens it.

exercises.prompt: What does 'наспра́вді' do in 'Здає́ться, що він бага́тий, але́ наспра́вді він бі́дний.'?
choices: It confirms what was just said.
It gives the cause of his being poor.
It sets what is really true against what seems true.
exercises.explanation: 'Наспра́вді' means 'in fact' and contradicts the appearance: he seems rich but is poor. 'Спра́вді', really, would confirm instead.

choices: Because of the cars, it is noisy in the village.
Thanks to the cars, it is quiet in the center.
Because of the cars, it is noisy in the center.

exercises.prompt_source: In my opinion, Taras is right.
Despite the rain, we went to the park.
I doubt that he will come.
I agree with you. (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: 'Пого́джуватися' takes 'з' with the instrumental, here 'з тобо́ю'. The short adjective 'зго́ден' is said by a man and 'зго́дна' by a woman.

exercises.prompt_source: It seems to me that Oksana is right.
answers: Мені́ здає́ться, що Окса́на ма́є ра́цію.
Мені́ здає́ться, що ра́цію ма́є Окса́на.
exercises.explanation: The person to whom something seems is in the dative, 'мені́', and 'to be right' is 'ма́ти ра́цію'.

exercises.prompt_source: Thanks to you, I found an apartment. (Sam to Oksana)
exercises.explanation: A cause with a good result is 'завдяки́' with the dative, 'тобі́'. Sam is a man, so the past form is 'знайшо́в'.

exercises.prompt_source: Because of the snow, we stayed at home.
exercises.explanation: A cause with an unwelcome result is 'че́рез' with the accusative, 'сніг'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why does Oksana doubt that Taras will like the village?
choices: There is no work there.
He loves the city so much.
He has no car.
exercises.explanation: Oksana says 'А я сумніва́юся, що тобі́ там сподо́бається. Ти так лю́биш мі́сто!'

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, how does Sam practice speaking online?
choices: He talks every week with a friend from Kharkiv.
He listens to lessons on his phone.
He talks with Iryna Petrivna in the evening.
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'У ме́не є по́друга з Ха́ркова, і ми гово́римо ко́жен ти́ждень.' He introduces this with 'Наспра́вді', because it contradicts the idea that online learning has no conversation.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'довкі́лля' written with two letters 'л'?
choices: The doubled letter before '-я' writes one long soft sound, as in 'життя́'.
The two letters belong to two different words.
The second 'л' is silent.
exercises.explanation: Neuter nouns in '-я' after a doubled consonant, like 'життя́' and 'пита́ння', write a long soft consonant: 'довкі́лля' [dɔwˈkʲilʲːɑ].

exercises.prompt: Why is 'о́тже' said with [d] in place of [t]?
choices: The 'т' is silent and the 'ж' is said [d].
The voiceless 'т' becomes voiced before the voiced 'ж', as 'к' does before 'з' in 'вокза́л'.
The stress changes the sound of the 'т'.
exercises.explanation: A voiceless consonant before a voiced one becomes voiced in Ukrainian. The spelling keeps 'т': 'о́тже' [ˈɔdʒɛ].

exercises.prompt: Why is 'незважа́ючи на' written as one word, while 'не зважа́ючи' in 'Він ішо́в, не зважа́ючи на дощ.' is two?
choices: One of the two spellings is old-fashioned.
The one-word spelling is used only at the start of a sentence.
'Незважа́ючи' is a preposition, written as one word; 'не' before the adverbial participle 'зважа́ючи' is written separately.
exercises.explanation: The preposition 'незважа́ючи на' grew out of the adverbial participle, and as a preposition it is written as one word. The participle itself, paying no heed, keeps 'не' apart.
